questions.q: Weekly revenue rises as you raise the price from ₹200 to ₹300 and then falls as you go on to ₹400. Which model is the natural first choice?
options: A straight line, because price is a single number
A degree-10 polynomial, because it will fit all the weeks most closely
Logistic regression, because revenue has a maximum
A degree-2 polynomial, because it can bend once to make a single peak
questions.why: One rise and one fall is a single bend, which is exactly what a quadratic (degree 2) captures. A straight line cannot find a peak. A degree-10 polynomial would fit the training weeks more closely but chase noise. Logistic regression is for yes/no targets, not a curved numeric relationship.

questions.q: The revenue model is **revenue ≈ −4.07 + 1.5579 × price − 0.0026714 × price²**. What does the negative coefficient on price² tell you?
options: Raising the price always lowers revenue
The curve is an arch, so the turning point is a maximum
The curve is a U, so the turning point is a minimum
The model has failed because coefficients should be positive
questions.why: When b₂ is negative the quadratic opens downwards (an arch), so the turning point is the highest revenue. A positive b₂, as in the fuel model, gives a U with a minimum. Revenue does rise with price at first, so "always lowers" misreads the curve by looking at one term instead of the whole shape.

questions.q: A farm fits **yield = 50 + 12x − 0.4x²**, where x is fertiliser in kg per plot. At what dose is predicted yield highest?
options: 15 kg
7.5 kg
30 kg
−15 kg
questions.why: The turning point is at −b₁ / (2b₂) = −12 / (2 × −0.4) = 15 kg, and b₂ < 0 makes it a maximum (yield 140). 30 kg forgets the factor of 2, 7.5 kg divides by 4b₂ instead of 2b₂, and −15 kg drops the minus sign in the formula.

questions.q: On 30 noisy fuel readings, a degree-1 polynomial has training RMSE 1.03 and cross-validated RMSE 1.05. What does this pair of numbers tell you?
options: The model is underfitting (high bias): it is too simple, so it is equally poor on training and new data
The model is overfitting, because the cross-validated error is higher
The model is ideal, because the training and validation errors are almost equal
Nothing, because RMSE cannot compare models of different degree
questions.why: Overfitting shows as a **gap** between low training error and higher validation error. Here both errors are large and close together, the signature of a model too stiff to follow the U-shape. Degree 2 cuts both to about 0.3. Small gap alone does not mean a good model; the level of error matters too.

questions.q: In the fuel model **fuel ≈ 13.5 − 0.2017 × speed + 0.001286 × speed²**, a colleague says "each extra km/h saves 0.2017 litres per 100 km". What is wrong?
options: Nothing: −0.2017 is the effect of one extra km/h
Changing speed also changes speed², so no single coefficient is the effect of speed; read the curve as a whole (shape, turning point, predictions)
The coefficient should be read in km per litre, not litres per 100 km
The coefficient is only valid at speed zero, so it should be ignored
questions.why: The effect of one extra km/h depends on where you start: below about 78 km/h fuel falls, above it fuel rises. The individual b's only make sense together. Holding speed² fixed while changing speed is impossible, which is why the "holding the others fixed" reading from multiple regression breaks down here.

questions.q: With 10 features and degree 3, including all cross terms such as x₁·x₂ and the intercept, how many columns does the polynomial model have?
questions.why: The number of terms of degree up to 3 in 10 variables is the combination C(13, 3) = 286. 30 counts only x, x² and x³ for each feature with no cross terms, and 1,000 is 10³, which is not how terms are counted. This explosion is why polynomial regression is best kept to one to three features.

questions.q: The fuel quadratic, fitted on speeds 40–120 km/h, predicts about 14.1 litres per 100 km at 160 km/h. How should you treat that number?
options: Trust it: the R² of 0.9997 shows the model is extremely accurate
Trust it, but only if you switch to a degree-4 polynomial
Distrust it because quadratics cannot predict values above the training maximum
Distrust it: it is an extrapolation, and a U-curve keeps rising outside the data just because of its shape
questions.why: The model never saw a speed above 120 km/h, so 160 km/h is pure extrapolation; the number comes from the formula, not from evidence. A near-perfect R² describes the fit inside the range only. Higher degrees make edge behaviour worse, not better. Quadratics can output any value; the issue is whether you should believe it.

questions.q: Interview question: "Cross-validation suggests you need degree 8 to capture the pattern. What do you do?"
options: Use degree 8 and report the training R²
Drop back to degree 1 because simpler is always better
Reach for a spline (or a ridge-regularised polynomial or tree model), which follows complex shapes without the wild edge swings of one high-degree polynomial
Remove the outliers until degree 2 fits
questions.why: Needing a high degree is a sign that a single polynomial is the wrong tool: it becomes unstable at the edges and numerically fragile. Splines join low-degree pieces at knots; regularisation tames the large coefficients. Dropping to degree 1 would underfit, and deleting data to fit a preferred model is not analysis.
